title: Sparkling Wines in Depth
description: From base wine to dosage: every choice that defines a sparkling wine, and the regions that master them.
L: Explain what makes a good base wine
Explain the role of reserve wines

A good base wine for sparkling is high in acidity, low in alcohol, around 10 to 11%, and neutral in flavour, so the second fermentation and lees can add character. Grapes are picked early, before sugar rises. Cool regions like Champagne, England and Tasmania give this naturally.

Whole bunches are pressed gently to avoid colour and bitterness from skins. In Champagne, 4,000 kg of grapes may give at most 2,550 litres. The first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, are the purest, with high acidity. The next 500 litres, the taille, are fruitier and less fine. Top houses often use only the cuvée.
In Champagne, what is the cuvée?
The first and purest pressing fraction
The cuvée is the first 2,050 litres from 4,000 kg of grapes, highest in acidity and finesse.

Houses keep reserve wines from earlier years to blend into their non-vintage, smoothing differences between vintages and adding depth. Some use 10 to 50% reserve wine, stored in tanks, barrels, or a perpetual solera-like system. This is how non-vintage Champagne keeps a consistent house style.
Reserve wines keep the house style
Grapes for sparkling base wine are usually picked later than grapes for still wine.
Not true. They're picked earlier, to keep high acidity and low sugar, since the second fermentation adds alcohol.
Base wines are acidic, low in alcohol and neutral
Gentle whole bunch pressing separates cuvée and taille
Reserve wines keep non-vintage blends consistent
Compare full and lower pressure styles

After blending, the base wine is mixed with the liqueur de tirage: sugar, about 24 g/l, selected yeast and riddling aids that help the sediment slide later. The bottle is closed with a crown cap. The yeast ferments the sugar, adding about 1.2 to 1.5% alcohol and producing carbon dioxide.

Each 4 grams of sugar per litre gives about 1 atmosphere of pressure. So 24 g/l produces about 6 atmospheres, typical of Champagne. Crémant has around 4 to 5; Pétillant naturel or frizzante wines much less. Cooler fermentation, around 12 degrees, gives finer bubbles and better integration.
In the second fermentation, about ____ grams of sugar per litre produce one atmosphere of pressure.
About 4 g/l per atmosphere, so 24 g/l gives around 6 atmospheres.

Pétillant naturel, or pét-nat, uses the ancestral method: wine is bottled before the first fermentation ends, so it finishes in bottle, trapping the gas. There's no added sugar or yeast, and often no disgorgement, leaving the wine cloudy. Bubbles are softer. Some appellations, like Gaillac and Limoux, have historic versions.
How is the ancestral method different from the traditional method?
There is only one fermentation, finished in bottle
The ancestral method bottles the wine while it is still fermenting, so there's no second fermentation.
Liqueur de tirage adds sugar and yeast for the second fermentation
About 4 g/l of sugar makes one atmosphere
Pét-nat finishes its single fermentation in bottle

After the second fermentation, the dead yeast cells slowly break down, releasing amino acids, mannoproteins and other compounds into the wine. This is autolysis. It begins after a few months and continues for years, adding bread, brioche, biscuit and nutty flavours, and a creamy texture, while the yeast also absorbs oxygen.
Dead yeast gives brioche and cream

Riddling moves the sediment into the neck. By hand, on wooden racks called pupitres, a remueur turns and tilts thousands of bottles a day, over several weeks. Gyropalettes, invented in Spain in the 1970s, do the same for 500 bottles at once in about a week. Some yeasts are encapsulated in beads to make it faster still.
Gyropalettes turn and tilt hundreds of bottles at once, replacing manual riddling.

Disgorgement ends lees ageing and starts a new phase. Before it, the wine is protected and evolves slowly. After it, oxygen enters, and the wine develops more toasty, nutty notes. Many producers now print the disgorgement date. Recently disgorged, or RD, wines are disgorged after long lees ageing, just before release.
The lees age the wine, are moved to the neck, removed, and the wine is topped up.
Autolysis releases bready, creamy notes from dead yeast
Riddling, by hand or gyropalette, moves sediment to the neck
The disgorgement date changes how the wine develops
Explain blanc de blancs, blanc de noirs and rosé

After disgorgement, the liqueur d'expédition, wine with sugar, tops up the bottle. It balances acidity and adds to the flavour development over time through Maillard reactions between sugar and amino acids. The trend is towards lower dosage, but very low dosage can taste austere in a young, high-acid wine.

Brut Nature has 0 to 3 g/l; Extra Brut up to 6; Brut up to 12; Extra Dry 12 to 17; Dry or Sec 17 to 32; Demi-Sec 32 to 50; Doux over 50. Blanc de Blancs is made only from white grapes, usually Chardonnay. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes. Rosé can be blended, with still red wine, or saignée.
Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs, Rosé
Which are true about Blanc de Noirs?
It's a white wine made from black grapes
It can use Pinot Noir and Meunier
Its colour comes from gentle pressing
Blanc de Noirs can be any sweetness level. Its pale colour comes from gentle pressing of black grapes.
A Demi-Sec Champagne is underrated with fruit tarts and spicy food. Extra Brut and Brut Nature shine with oysters and raw fish.
Which dosage term is drier: Extra Brut or Extra Dry?
Extra Brut has up to 6 g/l; Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/l.
Dosage balances acidity and helps flavour develop
Sweetness terms run from Brut Nature to Doux
Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs and Rosé describe grapes and colour

Champagne's main areas are the Montagne de Reims, famous for Pinot Noir; the Vallée de la Marne, for Meunier; the Côte des Blancs, for Chardonnay; and the Côte des Bar, further south, for Pinot Noir. The Côte de Sézanne also grows Chardonnay. Chalk subsoils, especially in the Côte des Blancs, give finesse.
Montagne, Vallée, Côte des Blancs, Côte des Bar

Champagne once ranked its 319 villages on a ladder, the échelle des crus, from 80% to 100%. Seventeen villages were Grand Cru at 100%, and 42 were Premier Cru, 90 to 99%. The percentage set the grape price. The pricing system ended in 2010, but the Grand Cru and Premier Cru names remain on labels.
How many Champagne villages hold Grand Cru status?
Seventeen villages are Grand Cru; 42 are Premier Cru.

Houses, or maisons, buy grapes from many growers and blend for a consistent style; they make most Champagne. Growers who make their own wine, called récoltant-manipulant and labelled RM, are a growing movement. Labels show these codes: NM for négociant-manipulant, RM for récoltant-manipulant, CM for co-operatives.
NM for houses; RM for growers
Match each label code to its meaning.
The small letters on the label tell you who made the wine.
Champagne's areas each favour a grape
The échelle des crus ranked villages; 17 are Grand Cru
NM houses blend; RM growers make wine from their own vines

Cava is Spain's traditional method wine, about 95% from Catalonia's Penedès. Macabeo, Xarel-lo and Parellada are the main grapes; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are allowed. The 2020 rules created zones and a top tier, Cava de Paraje Calificado, from single estates aged at least 36 months. Corpinnat producers left the DO for stricter organic rules.

Crémant is France's traditional method wine outside Champagne, made in eight AOPs, including Alsace, Burgundy, Loire, Jura, Limoux and Bordeaux. Rules require whole bunch pressing, a limit on juice yield, and at least 9 months on lees. Each uses local grapes: Chenin Blanc in the Loire, Pinot Blanc and Riesling in Alsace, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in Burgundy.
Eight crémant AOPs, 9 months on lees
Match each sparkling wine to its country.
The traditional method is used worldwide under many names.

Franciacorta, in Lombardy, needs 18 months on lees for non-vintage and is mainly Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Trentodoc, in Trentino, is mountain-grown. England's south, on chalk similar to Champagne's, has become a serious producer. South Africa's Méthode Cap Classique and Tasmania also make fine examples.
Crémant must spend at least 9 months on its lees.
Yes. That's the minimum for all French crémants.
Cava is mostly from Penedès, with a new single estate tier
Crémant is made in eight French AOPs with local grapes
Franciacorta, Trentodoc, England and Tasmania also excel

Explain each step of traditional method production
Put these stages of traditional method production in order.
Each step builds on the previous one.
What does autolysis give a sparkling wine?
Breakdown of dead yeast adds these flavours and texture.
Match each term to its meaning.
Champagne has precise words for each step.
A grower who makes their own Champagne carries the code ____ on the label.
Base wines are acidic and light; pressing fractions matter
Tirage creates pressure; autolysis adds flavour
Dosage sets sweetness; label codes reveal the maker
Champagne, Cava, crémant and others each have their rules
